newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia, in change, invites OSCE vote observers.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia, in change, invites OSCE vote observers.

text.p: The Yugoslav foreign minister on Thursday invited OSCE monitors to oversee September elections, hours after another senior official said they were not welcome without steps to restore Belgrade's membership in the security group.

The Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic had invited a delegation from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to the presidential and parliamentary elections in Serbia, one of Yugoslavia's two republics.

Hours earlier, a spokesman for the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) said OSCE monitors "have not been invited and will not be invited unless there are parallel activities leading to normalising Yugoslavia's status in the organisation".
Yugoslav membership in the OSCE was suspended in 1992 when the United Nations imposed an embargo against Belgrade for supporting separatist Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia's war, which ended in 1995.
Most sanctions were lifted after Slobodan Milosevic, then president of Serbia, helped secure the Dayton peace accords on Bosnia.

But Washington preserved an "outer wall" of sanctions, including membership in international organisations, until Belgrade meets several conditions, including respect for human rights and democratic reforms.

Some opposition parties have announced a boycott of the elections because they were denied equal access to the media, voting districts have been configured to favour the SPS, and the authorities refused to invite OSCE observers.
The biggest, the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), broke ranks with the rest of the opposition last week and said it would go ahead and campaign.
Other opposition parties accused the SPO of striking a deal with Milosevic, now president of Yugoslavia.
But on Thursday morning, the SPO said it was suspending its election campaign until Serbian authorities invite OSCE obervers.
A spokesman for the party said on Thursday evening that the SPO would now wait for a positive response to the invitation from the OSCE.

OSCE monitoring could improve the credibility of voting in Serbia in light of SPS election fraud last November that nullified opposition victories in Serbia's 14 biggest municipal districts, including Belgrade.

The opposition gains were reinstated only after three months of mass street protests and powerful international pressure on the authoritarian Milosevic and his Socialists to honour the outcome of a free election.
A boycott by the SPO would seriously damage SPS credibility since it would then face only the ultra-nationalist Radical Party in the elections.
It had made a move to stop a crackdown on independent media ahead of the elections but the opposition fears most independent stations will shut down once the voting is over.
The United States said on Tuesday it opposed a boycott of Serbian elections by opposition parties even though voting conditions are "grossly unfair".
Special U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, in Belgrade last weekend, chided the Serbian opposition, telling them: "It's stupid to boycott the elections."
Holbrooke said he told Milosevic that "over the long term, the support that the international community has for him will be determined by democratic conditions in Serbia."
But the U.S. State Department said on Tuesday "it doesn't appear that he (Milosevic) is going to make fundamental changes".
